claims.text: A PbTe-based alloy can serve as the crystalline semiconductor or thermoelectric material in which SRO precipitates are introduced to reduce lattice thermal conductivity.
Introducing SRO precipitates into the material will lower its lattice thermal conductivity.
Enhanced phonon-precipitate interactions reduce the phonon scattering time.
The initial PbTe-based alloy is homogeneous and possesses long-range order.
Phonon propagation in the initial homogeneous alloy is relatively unimpeded.
A controlled heat treatment or precipitation process can induce nanoscale short-range-ordered precipitates in the matrix.
Conducting the treatment between approximately room temperature and 700 K will ensure the stability and distribution of the SRO precipitates.
The treatment produces nanoscale SRO precipitates dispersed throughout the crystalline matrix.
SRO precipitates create additional interfaces in the matrix.
The additional precipitate interfaces enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering reduces the phonon mean free path.
A reduced phonon mean free path decreases the lattice component of thermal conductivity.
Samples containing induced SRO precipitates will have measurably lower lattice thermal conductivity than untreated homogeneous samples.
Untreated PbTe-based material has higher lattice thermal conductivity because it contains fewer phonon-scattering centers.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity effect depends on precipitate size, density, and distribution.
Precipitates that become too large will have a diminished effect on phonon scattering and thermal conductivity.
A precipitate volume fraction below a critical threshold will have a diminished effect on phonon scattering and thermal conductivity.
